attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own Substack post, stated as his view.

semantics.note: Faithful paraphrase of a retrospective claim. The weak quantifier 'not always' is preserved.

contract.note: The plain reading (surprising failures, and behaviour sometimes unlike humans', from about 2016 to the post) is ordinary and not stretched either way. 'Unpredictable' is reasonably read as unexpected failure, not randomness.

evidence.note: Controlled 2018 comparison: CNNs and humans classify the same images differently (texture vs shape bias, silhouettes). Within the period.
2017 researcher demonstration of robust, conspicuous misclassification of physical objects. Shows a surprising failure.
2019 study: humans could often anticipate machine labels on adversarial images. This limits a strong 'unpredictable' reading but does not refute 'not always human like'.

reviews.rationale: Primary studies inside 2016–2023 document surprising deep-learning failures and measurable differences from humans (e2, e3). e4 shows human intuition can partly predict machine errors. That qualifies but does not overturn the modest claim that deep learning is sometimes unexpected and not always human-like.

attribution.note: Marcus's own assertion in his post. The quotes from Gleave are separate and not scored.

semantics.note: The normalisation drops the claim that Gleave personally taught Pelrine and generalises 'Gleave's strategy'. The contract restores both elements, so the core claim is preserved.

contract.note: Splitting the claim fairly separates human transfer of the team's attack, continuity with the passing trick Marcus had just described, and personal teaching. The contract correctly treats missing evidence of personal teaching as a gap, not a contradiction.

evidence.note: Team's Feb 17, 2023 record: Pelrine learned the cyclic attack by studying game records, won unaided against several bots, and went 14-1 against a KGS bot.
Jan 2023 paper version: the cyclic attack is qualitatively different from the pass trick. So the human win did not carry the passing strategy Marcus described.

reviews.rationale: Part of the claim holds: a human co-author learned the team's adversarial attack and won repeatedly, so it was no fluke (e8). Part fails: the winning attack was the cyclic one, not the passing trick Marcus had just described (e9). Gleave personally teaching Pelrine is not shown; the records point to learning from game records.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his post.

semantics.note: Faithful. 'Don't work the way people do' matches 'isn't the same as what people do'.

contract.note: The plain reading (several demonstrations of substantial adversarial vulnerability, with human behaviour or robustness differing) is ordinary. It does not stretch the claim into one about shared mechanisms.

evidence.note: 2017: adversarial sentences cut F1 from 75% to 36% across 16 models, while direct human testing showed smaller losses.
2018: targeted audio attack with 100% success on DeepSpeech, a different domain. The human comparison here is weaker (perceptual similarity only).
2018: some strongly transferring adversarial images influenced time-limited humans. This limits any claim of universal human immunity but does not erase differences shown elsewhere.

reviews.rationale: Independent primary studies across text and audio show large adversarial failures. At least one tests humans directly and finds much greater robustness (e5, e6). e7 shows some overlap under restricted viewing. That qualifies but does not contradict the claim that attacks repeatedly exposed weaknesses and behaviour unlike people's.

attribution.note: Marcus's own concluding statement in his post.

semantics.note: This is a rhetorical, evaluative summation ('poignant reminder') about what a term implies, not a measurable historical observation. 'Conceptual depth' has no measure.

contract.note: The contract adopts a weak reading (architecture does not guarantee understanding) and discards the force of 'just' and 'at all'. That makes the claim near-tautological, stretched in the speaker's favour. An informed reader takes it as a denial of real conceptual depth, which is unmeasured.

evidence.note: 2015 review describes deep learning as layered models that learn levels of abstraction. It is a definition and does not measure conceptual depth.
2016 textbook ties the term itself to a learned hierarchy of concepts. This cuts against 'just layers' but does not establish understanding.
Nov 2022 Go paper shows surprising failure modes. It does not measure conceptual depth.

reviews.rationale: This is an evaluative characterisation, not a testable observation. On the contract's weak reading it is trivially true. On the ordinary reading (deep learning lacks real conceptual depth), no measure exists. The evidence also points both ways: e2 links the term to concept hierarchies. It cannot be fairly scored.
